title: Called to the House
logline: A village monk is called to house after house where someone is close to death, walking the same roads again and again to sit with families he barely has time to know.

object.note: Object 8 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: When speed has done what it can, someone still comes: a village monk walking to house after house where someone is close to death.

thread_out.thread: Presence at the end of lives turns inward: a teacher's brief evening meetings on a silent retreat, trying to gauge how deep each student has gone.

requirements: A rural temple whose monk regularly performs this pastoral role and is willing to be followed
Families willing to have the monk's visit, not the dying person, filmed
Full, ongoing consent, with the dying person's own wishes given priority

lesson.in_simple_terms: The texts treat dying as one more act of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching or remembering, so what reaches a dying person's senses still reaches them. They also count a good friend at the bedside, who helps someone recall the good they have done, as a real help.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: මරණාසන්න මොහොත ද දැකීම, ඇසීම, සුවඳ දැනීම, ස්පර්ශය හෝ සිහි කිරීම වැනි සාමාන්‍ය අත්දැකීමක් බැවින්, මියයන කෙනෙකු ළඟ සිටින කල්‍යාණ මිත්‍රයෙකු ඔවුන් කළ යහපත සිහි කරවීම සැබෑ උපකාරයක් බව ග්‍රන්ථ කියයි.
lesson.the_teaching: The Abhidhamma describes a near-death mental process that can run through any of the five sense doors or the mind door; because the physical base of mind is weak then, only five impulsion moments arise instead of seven. The Margaya gives examples: someone dying while hearing a teaching recited, smelling incense that was offered, or feeling another person's touch. In the order in which actions ripen, weighty action comes first, then action done or recalled near death, then habitual action, then reserve action, and the Margaya concludes that it is very helpful to have a good friend who helps the dying do or recall something good.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The call arrives, the monk sets off again on the same roads, and a front room has been rearranged around a sickbed. The chant is heard through a doorway, as the dying person might hear it, and the walk home leaves the viewer weighing what the visit could and could not do. The monk's own words about the work carry the rest.

key_terms.en: death-proximate kamma (done or recalled near death)

lesson.caution: It does not mean a chant or a visit can secure where someone goes, or that a calm or troubled death shows what kind of person they were; the texts place the weight on what arises in the dying person's own mind.
lesson.builds_on: When the ambulance's speed has done what it can, this film adds that the end of a life is still lived through the senses, and that the company at the bedside belongs inside the teaching.
